statement: If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational straight lines arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.
heath_proof: For let two medial areas AB, CD incommensurable with one another be added together; I say that the “side” of the area AD is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas. For AB is either greater or less than CD. First, if it so chance, let AB be greater than CD. Let the rational straight line EF be set out, and to EF let there be applied the rectangle EG equal to AB and producing EH as breadth, and the rectangle HI equal to CD and producing HK as breadth. Now, since each of the areas AB, CD is medial, therefore each of the areas EG, HI is also medial. And they are applied to the rational straight line FE, producing EH, HK as breadth; therefore each of the straight lines EH, HK is rational and incommensurable in length with EF. [X. 22] And, since AB is incommensurable with CD, and AB is equal to EG, and CD to HI, therefore EG is also incommensurable with HI. But, as EG is to HI, so is EH to HK; [VI. 1] therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HK. [X. 11] Therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EK is binomial. [X. 36] But the square on EH is greater than the square on HK either by the square on a straight line commensurable with EH or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. First, let the square on it be greater by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with itself. Now neither of the straight lines EH, HK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out; therefore EK is a third binomial. [X. Deff. II. 3] But EF is rational; and, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the third binomial, the “side” of the area is a second bimedial; [X. 56] therefore the “side” of EI, that is, of AD, is a second bimedial. Next, let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Now each of the straight lines EH, HK is incommensurable in length with EF; therefore EK is a sixth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 6] But, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the “side” of the area is the side of the sum of two medial areas; [X. 59] so that the “side” of the area AD is also the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Statement:** If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational straight lines arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be two medial areas incommensurable with one another (each equal to the square on a medial straight line), and let AD be the area made up of both. It is required to prove that the straight line which produces AD, that is, the side of the square equal to AD [D10.1.4], is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line EF [D10.1.3]. To EF apply the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth; and to HG, the side of EG opposite to EF, apply the rectangle HI equal to CD, producing HK as breadth [1.44]. Since HG is opposite to EF in the parallelogram EG, HG = EF [1.34]; and EH, HK lie in one straight line EK, so that the whole EI is the rectangle contained by EF and EK.

**Step 3.** Since AB is a medial area and EG = AB, EG is the square on a medial straight line applied to the rational straight line EF; therefore its breadth EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Likewise HI = CD is a medial area applied to HG, which is rational, being equal to EF; therefore HK is rational and incommensurable in length with HG, that is, with EF [10.22].

**Step 4.** The rectangles EG and HI are under the same height EF (= HG) and stand on the bases EH, HK; therefore EG : HI = EH : HK [6.1]. But EG = AB and HI = CD, and AB is incommensurable with CD; therefore EG is incommensurable with HI, and hence EH is incommensurable in length with HK [10.11].

**Step 5.** EH is rational and not commensurable in length with EF; therefore it is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3], so that the square on EH is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]. In the same way the square on HK is commensurable with the square on EF. Therefore the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HK [10.12], that is, EH and HK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Since by Step 4 they are incommensurable in length, EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 6.** Therefore EK, the sum of EH and HK, is a binomial straight line [10.36], divided into its terms EH, HK at the point H.

**Step 7.** EH and HK are unequal: equal straight lines measure one another and are therefore commensurable [D10.1.1], whereas EH, HK are incommensurable. Let EH be the greater term. The square on EH exceeds the square on HK by the square on some straight line, and this straight line is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with EH; so two cases arise.

**Step 8.** Case (i): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH. By Step 3 neither term EH nor HK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out. Therefore EK is a third binomial [D10.2.3].

**Step 9.** The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the third binomial EK; therefore the side of EI, the straight line whose square is equal to EI, is a second bimedial [10.56].

**Step 10.** Case (ii): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Again neither term is commensurable in length with EF; therefore EK is a sixth binomial [D10.2.6].

**Step 11.** The area EI is then contained by the rational straight line EF and the sixth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.59].

**Step 12.** But EG = AB and HI = CD; adding these equals, EI = EG + HI = AB + CD = AD [CN2]. Therefore the straight line whose square is equal to AD is the very side of EI found in Step 9 or Step 11.

**Step 13.** Hence, when two medial areas incommensurable with one another are added together, the straight line which produces the sum is, according as the square on the greater term of EK exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line commensurable or incommensurable in length with the greater, either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas. These are the two irrational straight lines not obtained from the sum of a rational and a medial area. Q.E.D.
